The amygdala processes fear/emotional salience; the hypothalamus expresses emotion via autonomic/endocrine output; the cingulate is involved in emotional awareness/regulation.

optWhy.A: Correct. Hippocampus = context/declarative memory of emotion.
optWhy.B: Amygdala = fear/emotional salience.
optWhy.C: Hypothalamus = autonomic/endocrine expression of emotion.
optWhy.D: Cingulate gyrus = emotional awareness/regulation.

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis stress response proceeds as:
why: The HPA axis: hypothalamus releases CRH → anterior pituitary releases ACTH → adrenal cortex releases cortisol. The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline (sympathetic, not HPA). The order is hypothalamus → pituitary → adrenal cortex.

optWhy.A: Correct. CRH → ACTH → cortisol (HPA axis).
optWhy.B: Adrenal medulla releases adrenaline; order is wrong for HPA.
optWhy.C: Order is reversed; hypothalamus (CRH) comes first.
optWhy.D: Adrenal medulla (adrenaline) is sympathetic, not part of the HPA cortisol axis.

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome comprises the stages:
why: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) describes the body's response to prolonged stress in three stages: alarm, resistance, and exhaustion. Excitement/plateau/orgasm/resolution is Masters and Johnson's sexual response cycle; denial/anger/bargaining/depression/acceptance is Kübler-Ross's stages of grief; infancy/adulthood are developmental stages.

optWhy.A: Correct. GAS = alarm, resistance, exhaustion.
optWhy.B: This is Masters and Johnson's sexual response cycle.
optWhy.C: This is Kübler-Ross's stages of grief.
optWhy.D: These are developmental stages, not GAS.

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: Compared with adrenaline, cortisol:

options.text: Acts more slowly and has longer-lasting effects (hormonal via bloodstream)
Acts within milliseconds via direct neural wiring
Is released by the adrenal medulla only

why: Adrenaline (adrenal medulla) acts rapidly via sympathetic neural activation (seconds). Cortisol (adrenal cortex, via HPA axis) acts more slowly (minutes to hours) and has longer-lasting hormonal effects via the bloodstream. Cortisol increases (not decreases) blood glucose.

optWhy.A: Correct. Cortisol = slower, longer-lasting hormonal action via bloodstream.
optWhy.B: Millisecond direct neural wiring = adrenaline/sympathetic, not cortisol.
optWhy.C: Adrenaline is adrenal medulla; cortisol is adrenal cortex.
optWhy.D: Cortisol increases blood glucose (glucocorticoid).

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: During fear, sympathetic activation produces:

options.text: Increased heart rate, pupil dilation, and inhibited digestion
Decreased heart rate, pupil constriction, and increased digestion

why: Fear activates the sympathetic nervous system (fight-or-flight): increased heart rate, pupil dilation, bronchodilation, inhibited digestion, and adrenal medulla adrenaline release. The opposite (decreased HR, pupil constriction, increased digestion) is parasympathetic.

optWhy.A: Correct. Sympathetic fear response = increased HR, pupil dilation, inhibited digestion.
optWhy.B: This is parasympathetic (rest-and-digest), not sympathetic fear.
optWhy.C: Fear produces clear sympathetic physiological changes.
optWhy.D: Skeletal muscle is activated (fight/flight), not relaxed.

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: The amygdala is central to fear conditioning.
reason: The amygdala receives sensory input and coordinates fear responses (freezing, escape, autonomic arousal) via outputs to the hypothalamus and periaqueductal gray.

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false
Assertion is false but Reason is true

why: Both are true and the Reason explains the Assertion: the amygdala is central to fear conditioning and orchestrates fear responses (freezing, escape, autonomic arousal) via outputs to the hypothalamus (autonomic/endocrine) and periaqueductal gray (behavioral).

optWhy.A: Correct. Both true; amygdala outputs to hypothalamus/PAG explain its central fear role.
optWhy.B: The Reason is the correct explanation.
optWhy.C: The Reason is true.
optWhy.D: The Assertion is true.

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: Match the emotion theory (List-I) to its core sequence/proponent (List-II).
why: James-Lange = bodily changes → emotion (1). Cannon-Bard = emotion and arousal simultaneous via thalamus (2). Schachter-Singer = arousal + cognitive label (3). Lazarus = cognitive appraisal → emotion (4).

optWhy.A: Correct. A-1 (James-Lange), B-2 (Cannon-Bard), C-3 (Schachter-Singer), D-4 (Lazarus).
optWhy.B: James-Lange is bodily changes→emotion (1), not simultaneous (2).
optWhy.C: Schachter-Singer is arousal+label (3), not simultaneous (2); Cannon-Bard is simultaneous (2), not bodily changes (1).
optWhy.D: Lazarus is appraisal→emotion (4), not bodily changes (1).

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: Match the limbic structure (List-I) to its emotion-related function (List-II).
listII: 3. Autonomic and endocrine expression of emotion
why: Amygdala = fear processing and fear conditioning (1). Hippocampus = context/declarative memory of emotion (2). Hypothalamus = autonomic/endocrine expression of emotion (3). Cingulate gyrus = emotional awareness and regulation (4).

optWhy.A: Correct. A-1 (amygdala fear), B-2 (hippocampus context), C-3 (hypothalamus expression), D-4 (cingulate awareness/regulation).
optWhy.B: Amygdala is fear (1), not context (2).
optWhy.C: Hypothalamus is expression (3), not context (2); hippocampus is context (2), not expression (3).
optWhy.D: Cingulate is awareness/regulation (4), not fear (1).

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: Which statements are correct?
statements: 1. James-Lange theory proposes that bodily changes precede emotion.
2. Cannon-Bard theory proposes simultaneous emotional experience and arousal.
3. Schachter-Singer theory requires both arousal and a cognitive label.
4. Lazarus theory proposes that emotion precedes appraisal.
why: Statement 1 is correct (James-Lange: bodily changes precede emotion). Statement 2 is correct (Cannon-Bard: simultaneous experience and arousal). Statement 3 is correct (Schachter-Singer: arousal + cognitive label). Statement 4 is incorrect: Lazarus proposes appraisal → emotion, not emotion → appraisal.

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct; statement 4 is false.
optWhy.B: Statement 4 is false; omits statements 2 and 3.
optWhy.C: Omits statement 1, which is correct.
optWhy.D: Statement 4 is false; Lazarus is appraisal → emotion.

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: Which statements are correct?
statements: 1. The HPA axis is hypothalamus (CRH) → anterior pituitary (ACTH) → adrenal cortex (cortisol).
2. Cortisol mobilizes glucose and suppresses immune function during stress.
3. Adrenaline acts more slowly than cortisol.
4. The sympathetic adrenal medulla releases adrenaline during fight-or-flight.
why: Statement 1 is correct (HPA axis = CRH → ACTH → cortisol). Statement 2 is correct (cortisol mobilizes glucose and suppresses immune function). Statement 3 is incorrect: adrenaline acts faster than cortisol (neural vs hormonal). Statement 4 is correct (sympathetic adrenal medulla releases adrenaline in fight-or-flight).

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 2 and 4.
optWhy.C: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 1 and 4.
optWhy.D: Statement 3 is false; adrenaline acts faster than cortisol.

key: HPA axis vs sympathetic adrenal medulla

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: A patient with bilateral amygdala damage is shown fearful faces. The expected result is:

options.text: Impaired recognition of fear in faces, despite intact recognition of other emotions
Complete inability to recognize any emotion

why: Bilateral amygdala damage (e.g., Urbach-Wiethe disease) impairs fear recognition and fear conditioning while sparing recognition of many other emotions, demonstrating the amygdala's specific role in fear. It does not enhance fear recognition or abolish all emotion recognition.

optWhy.A: Correct. Amygdala damage → impaired fear recognition, other emotions spared.
optWhy.B: Amygdala damage impairs, not enhances, fear recognition.
optWhy.C: Other emotion recognition is largely spared.
optWhy.D: Fear recognition is impaired.

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: Chronic stress produces prolonged HPA activation and elevated cortisol. The expected consequence is:

options.text: Suppressed immune function and increased susceptibility to illness (Selye exhaustion phase)

why: Chronic stress → prolonged cortisol elevation → suppressed immune function (Selye's exhaustion phase), increasing susceptibility to illness. Cortisol does not enhance immunity indefinitely, has clear effects, and increases (not decreases) blood glucose.

optWhy.A: Correct. Chronic cortisol suppresses immunity (exhaustion phase → illness susceptibility).
optWhy.B: Cortisol suppresses, not enhances, immunity.
optWhy.C: Chronic stress/cortisol clearly affects immunity.
optWhy.D: Cortisol increases blood glucose (glucocorticoid).

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Emotion experience and emotion expression can be dissociated.
reason: The hypothalamus mediates emotional expression (autonomic/endocrine output) while cortical/limbic circuits contribute to subjective experience.

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false
Assertion is false but Reason is true

why: Both are true and the Reason explains the Assertion: emotion experience (subjective feeling) and expression (autonomic/endocrine/behavioral output via hypothalamus) are separable; one can occur without the other.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both true; hypothalamus expression vs cortical/limbic experience explains dissociation.
optWhy.B: The Reason is the correct explanation.
optWhy.C: The Reason is true.
optWhy.D: The Assertion is true.

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: The facial-feedback hypothesis is consistent with James-Lange because both:

options.text: Hold that bodily feedback influences emotional experience
Hold that cognition always precedes emotion
Deny any role for bodily changes in emotion

why: The facial-feedback hypothesis (facial expressions influence emotional experience) is consistent with James-Lange because both hold that bodily feedback influences emotional experience. Neither holds cognition always precedes emotion, denies bodily changes, or applies only to fear.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both facial-feedback and James-Lange = bodily feedback influences emotional experience.
optWhy.B: Neither holds cognition always precedes emotion.
optWhy.C: Both affirm a role for bodily changes.
optWhy.D: Both apply to emotion generally, not only fear.

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: A person with spinal cord injury (reduced bodily feedback) reports attenuated emotional intensity. This is consistent with:

options.text: James-Lange theory (bodily feedback contributes to emotion intensity)
Cannon-Bard theory (simultaneity regardless of bodily feedback)
Schachter-Singer theory (arousal + label regardless of body)

why: Reduced bodily feedback after spinal cord injury attenuating emotional intensity is consistent with James-Lange, which holds that bodily feedback contributes to emotion intensity. Cannon-Bard (simultaneity), Schachter-Singer (arousal+label), and Lazarus (appraisal) do not predict attenuation from reduced bodily feedback as directly.

optWhy.A: Correct. James-Lange predicts attenuated emotion with reduced bodily feedback.
optWhy.B: Cannon-Bard predicts simultaneity regardless of bodily feedback.
optWhy.C: Schachter-Singer focuses on arousal+label, not bodily-feedback attenuation.
optWhy.D: Lazarus focuses on appraisal, not bodily feedback.

key: Spinal cord injury emotion intensity James-Lange

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: Which statement best reflects the modern view of the limbic system?

options.text: Emotion is distributed across interconnected limbic and cortical networks, not a single 'limbic system' center
The limbic system is a single discrete center for all emotion
Only the amygdala is involved in emotion

why: Modern neuroscience views emotion as distributed across interconnected limbic (amygdala, hippocampus, hypothalamus, cingulate) and cortical (prefrontal, insula) networks, rather than a single 'limbic system' center or only the amygdala or purely cortex. The limbic system concept (MacLean) is a historical framework.

optWhy.A: Correct. Modern view = distributed limbic and cortical networks for emotion.
optWhy.B: Emotion is not a single discrete limbic center.
optWhy.C: Multiple limbic and cortical structures, not only amygdala, are involved.
optWhy.D: Emotion involves subcortical limbic structures, not purely cortex.

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: Researchers block central amygdala output to the periaqueductal gray in rats. The expected result is:

options.text: Reduced freezing and escape behaviors (fear expression impaired)

why: Central amygdala output to the periaqueductal gray drives fear expression behaviors (freezing, escape). Blocking this output reduces freezing/escape (fear expression impaired) without necessarily eliminating fear learning. It does not enhance freezing, have no effect, or enhance appetite.

optWhy.A: Correct. Blocking central amygdala→PAG output reduces freezing/escape (fear expression).
optWhy.B: Blocking output reduces, not enhances, freezing/escape.
optWhy.C: Central amygdala→PAG clearly affects fear behavior.
optWhy.D: Appetite is not the fear-expression output.

key: Central amygdala to PAG fear expression

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: A patient with Cushing's syndrome (chronic cortisol excess) shows:

options.text: Suppressed immunity, hyperglycemia, and central obesity
Decreased blood glucose and increased muscle mass

why: Cushing's syndrome (chronic cortisol excess) causes hyperglycemia (cortisol increases blood glucose), suppressed immunity, and central obesity (fat redistribution). It does not enhance immunity/weight loss, has clear physiological changes, and increases (not decreases) blood glucose and muscle wasting (not increased muscle mass).

optWhy.A: Correct. Cushing's = hyperglycemia, suppressed immunity, central obesity.
optWhy.B: Cortisol suppresses immunity and promotes central obesity, not weight loss.
optWhy.C: Chronic cortisol excess has clear physiological effects.
optWhy.D: Cortisol increases blood glucose and causes muscle wasting, not the reverse.

topic: Biological basis of emotion and hormonal regulation
stem: In a fear-conditioning experiment, a tone (CS) is paired with a shock (US) until the tone alone elicits freezing (CR). Lesioning the amygdala after conditioning:

options.text: Impairs expression of the conditioned fear response (freezing)
Has no effect because learning is in the cortex
Eliminates the unconditioned response to shock permanently

why: The amygdala is essential for expressing conditioned fear (freezing). Lesioning it after conditioning impairs the expression of the conditioned fear response. It does not enhance fear, leave learning intact in cortex (amygdala is the key fear site), or permanently eliminate the unconditioned shock response (which is mediated by reflex arcs).

optWhy.A: Correct. Amygdala lesion impairs expression of conditioned fear (freezing).
optWhy.B: Amygdala lesion reduces, not enhances, fear expression.
optWhy.C: Amygdala is critical for fear conditioning, not cortex alone.
optWhy.D: The unconditioned shock response is reflexive and not permanently eliminated by amygdala lesion.

stem: Mendel's law of segregation states that:

options.text: Allele pairs separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries one allele
All alleles are expressed equally in the phenotype
Genes on the same chromosome are always inherited together

why: Mendel's law of segregation: during gamete formation (meiosis), the two alleles for a gene separate so each gamete receives only one allele. Equal expression relates to dominance (not segregation); linked genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together (linkage, not segregation); environment is not the basis of segregation.

optWhy.A: Correct. Allele pairs separate during gamete formation (meiosis).
optWhy.B: Equal expression relates to dominance/codominance, not segregation.
optWhy.C: Linked genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together (linkage), not segregation.
optWhy.D: Environment is not the basis of Mendel's law of segregation.

stem: Genotype differs from phenotype in that genotype:

options.text: Is the genetic makeup, whereas phenotype is the observable characteristic
Is the observable characteristic, whereas genotype is the genetic makeup
Changes with the environment, whereas phenotype is fixed
Is only relevant for recessive traits

why: Genotype = the genetic makeup (alleles an organism carries). Phenotype = the observable characteristic/trait (result of genotype + environment). Genotype does not change with environment; genotype matters for dominant and recessive traits.

optWhy.A: Correct. Genotype = genetic makeup; phenotype = observable characteristic.
optWhy.B: This reverses genotype and phenotype.
optWhy.C: Genotype is fixed at conception; phenotype can change with environment.
optWhy.D: Genotype is relevant for both dominant and recessive traits.

stem: If both parents are carriers (heterozygous) for an autosomal recessive disorder, the chance that each child is affected is:
why: Two carriers (Aa x Aa) produce offspring: 25% AA (unaffected), 50% Aa (carrier, unaffected), 25% aa (affected). So each child has a 25% chance of being affected.

optWhy.A: Correct. Aa x Aa -> 25% aa (affected).
optWhy.B: 50% are carriers (Aa), not affected.
optWhy.C: 75% are unaffected (AA + Aa), not affected.
optWhy.D: Not 100%; only 25% affected.

stem: X-linked (sex-linked) inheritance differs from autosomal inheritance in that:

options.text: The gene is on the X chromosome, so males (XY) express the trait with one copy
The gene is on an autosome, so both sexes are affected equally

why: X-linked genes are on the X chromosome; males (XY) have only one X, so a single recessive allele expresses the trait (e.g., red-green color blindness). Autosomal genes are on non-sex chromosomes and affect both sexes more equally. X-linked traits do not necessarily skip every generation nor are they always dominant.

optWhy.A: Correct. X-linked gene; males (XY) express with one copy.
optWhy.B: Autosomal genes are on non-sex chromosomes (this describes autosomal, not X-linked).
optWhy.C: X-linked traits do not necessarily skip every generation.
optWhy.D: X-linked traits can be dominant or recessive.

stem: Down syndrome is caused by:
why: Down syndrome is trisomy 21 (three copies of chromosome 21). Monosomy X (45,X) = Turner syndrome. 47,XXY = Klinefelter syndrome. 47,XYY = XYY syndrome.

optWhy.A: Correct. Down syndrome = trisomy 21.
optWhy.B: Monosomy X (45,X) = Turner syndrome.
optWhy.C: 47,XXY = Klinefelter syndrome.
optWhy.D: 47,XYY = XYY syndrome.

stem: Turner syndrome differs from Klinefelter syndrome in that Turner:

options.text: Is monosomy X (45,X) in females, whereas Klinefelter is 47,XXY in males
Is 47,XXY in males, whereas Klinefelter is monosomy X in females
Affects only males in both syndromes

why: Turner syndrome = 45,X (monosomy X) in females. Klinefelter syndrome = 47,XXY in males. Down syndrome = trisomy 21.

optWhy.A: Correct. Turner = 45,X (females); Klinefelter = 47,XXY (males).
optWhy.B: This reverses Turner and Klinefelter.
optWhy.C: Turner affects females (45,X), not only males.
optWhy.D: Extra chromosome 21 = Down syndrome, not Turner/Klinefelter.

stem: The claim that XYY males constitute a 'criminal syndrome' is best regarded as:

options.text: A debunked myth; XYY males are mostly of normal intelligence and not inherently criminal
A well-established genetic cause of criminality
True only for XYY males with low socioeconomic status

why: The claim that XYY (47,XYY) males are a 'criminal syndrome' is a debunked myth; early biased studies in prison populations overstated the link. XYY males are mostly of normal intelligence and are not inherently criminal. It is not true only for low-SES XYY males nor proven by adoption studies.

optWhy.A: Correct. XYY 'criminal syndrome' is a debunked myth.
optWhy.B: Not a well-established genetic cause of criminality.
optWhy.C: Not true only for low-SES XYY males; the syndrome claim is debunked.
optWhy.D: Not proven by adoption studies.

stem: Heritability (h^2) is best defined as:

options.text: The proportion of phenotypic variation in a population attributable to genetic variation
The proportion of an individual's trait that is genetic
The probability a trait is inherited from parents
A fixed value that applies across all environments

why: Heritability is the proportion of phenotypic VARIATION in a given population that is attributable to genetic variation in that population/environment. It is NOT the proportion of an individual's trait that is genetic, not a probability of inheritance, and not fixed across environments (it changes with environmental variation).

optWhy.A: Correct. Heritability = proportion of phenotypic variation in a population due to genetic variation.
optWhy.B: Heritability is not the proportion of an individual's trait that is genetic.
optWhy.C: Heritability is not a probability of inheritance.
optWhy.D: Heritability is environment-dependent, not a fixed value across environments.

stem: If monozygotic (MZ) twins are much more concordant than dizygotic (DZ) twins for a trait, this suggests:

options.text: A genetic contribution to the trait (but not 100% determinism)
MZ twins share more environment than DZ twins, so genetics is irrelevant

why: MZ twins share ~100% of genes; DZ twins share ~50%. Higher MZ than DZ concordance suggests a genetic contribution. It does not mean the trait is entirely genetic (MZ concordance is rarely 100%, environment matters), nor entirely environmental, nor that MZ share more environment in a way that negates genetics.

optWhy.A: Correct. Higher MZ than DZ concordance suggests genetic contribution.
optWhy.B: MZ concordance is rarely 100%; environment matters (not entirely genetic).
optWhy.C: Higher MZ concordance indicates genetic, not purely environmental, influence.
optWhy.D: MZ/DZ comparison is specifically designed to infer genetic influence.

key: Twin study MZ vs DZ concordance

stem: An adoption study finding that adopted children's IQ correlates more with their biological than adoptive parents suggests:

options.text: Genetic influence on IQ (shared environment of adoptive home is weaker)
Adoptive parents have no influence on IQ

why: If adopted children correlate more with biological parents (shared genes) than adoptive parents (shared rearing environment), this suggests genetic influence on IQ. It does not mean IQ is entirely genetic or environmental, nor that adoptive parents have no influence (shared environment matters, especially in childhood).

optWhy.A: Correct. Greater correlation with biological parents suggests genetic influence.
optWhy.B: Not entirely genetic; shared environment matters.
optWhy.C: Not entirely environmental; genetic influence suggested.
optWhy.D: Adoptive parents may still influence IQ; the finding is comparative, not absolute.

key: Adoption study IQ biological vs adoptive parents

stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Heritability of 0.60 for IQ means 60% of the differences among people in a population are attributable to genetic differences.
reason: Heritability is a population statistic about variation, not a statement that 60% of any one person's IQ is genetic.

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false
Assertion is false but Reason is true

why: Both are true and the Reason explains the Assertion: heritability of 0.60 means 60% of the VARIANCE in IQ in that population is attributable to genetic variation; it is a population statistic, not a claim that 60% of any individual's IQ is genetic.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both true; heritability is population-level variation, not individual-level genetic proportion.
optWhy.B: The Reason is the correct explanation.
optWhy.C: The Reason is true.
optWhy.D: The Assertion is true.

stem: Match the chromosomal anomaly (List-I) to its karyotype/features (List-II).
why: Down syndrome = trisomy 21 (1); Turner = 45,X monosomy X in females (2); Klinefelter = 47,XXY in males (3); Fragile X = FMR1 gene mutation, X-linked intellectual disability (4).

optWhy.A: Correct. A-1 (Down), B-2 (Turner), C-3 (Klinefelter), D-4 (Fragile X).
optWhy.B: Down is trisomy 21 (1), not 45,X (2).
optWhy.C: Turner is 45,X (2), not 47,XXY (3); Klinefelter is 47,XXY (3), not 45,X (2).
optWhy.D: Fragile X is FMR1 (4), not Down (1); Down is trisomy 21 (1), not Fragile X.

stem: Match the inheritance pattern (List-I) to an example (List-II).
why: Autosomal dominant = Huntington's disease (1); autosomal recessive = cystic fibrosis (2); X-linked recessive = red-green color blindness (3); multifactorial = height/intelligence (genes + environment) (4).

optWhy.A: Correct. A-1 (Huntington's), B-2 (cystic fibrosis), C-3 (color blindness), D-4 (height/intelligence).
optWhy.B: Autosomal dominant is Huntington's (1), not cystic fibrosis (2).
optWhy.C: Autosomal recessive is cystic fibrosis (2), not color blindness (3); X-linked recessive is color blindness (3), not cystic fibrosis (2).
optWhy.D: Multifactorial is height/intelligence (4), not autosomal dominant (4).

stem: Which statements are correct?
statements: 1. The nature-nurture debate is best understood as gene-environment interaction, not either/or.
2. Heritability estimates apply to a specific population and environment.
3. Genes determine behavior directly and independently of environment.
4. Gene-environment correlation means people select environments correlated with their genotype.
why: Statement 1 is correct (nature-nurture = interaction, not either/or). Statement 2 is correct (heritability is population/environment-specific). Statement 3 is incorrect: genes do not determine behavior directly and independently of environment. Statement 4 is correct (gene-environment correlation = rGE, people select environments correlated with their genotype).

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 2 and 4.
optWhy.C: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 1 and 4.
optWhy.D: Statement 3 is false; genes do not determine behavior independently of environment.

stem: Which statements are correct?
statements: 1. Twin studies compare MZ (near 100% shared genes) and DZ (~50% shared genes) concordance.
2. Adoption studies compare adopted children to biological and adoptive parents.
3. A high MZ concordance proves a trait is 100% genetic.
4. Heritability can change if the environment changes.
why: Statement 1 is correct (twin studies compare MZ vs DZ concordance). Statement 2 is correct (adoption studies compare to biological and adoptive parents). Statement 3 is incorrect: high MZ concordance does NOT prove 100% genetic (MZ concordance is rarely 100%). Statement 4 is correct (heritability changes with environment).

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 2 and 4.
optWhy.C: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 1 and 4.
optWhy.D: Statement 3 is false; high concordance does not prove 100% genetic.

stem: A researcher compares MZ twins reared apart and finds IQ concordance of 0.70, much higher than DZ twins reared together. The strongest conclusion is:

options.text: Genetic influence on IQ is substantial (but environment still matters)
IQ is 70% genetic for each individual
Shared rearing environment has no effect on IQ
MZ twins reared apart are genetically different

why: High MZ reared-apart concordance (0.70) much higher than DZ reared-together indicates substantial genetic influence on IQ. It does NOT mean 70% of an individual's IQ is genetic (heritability is population-level), shared rearing environment still matters, and MZ twins are genetically near-identical (not different).

optWhy.A: Correct. Substantial genetic influence on IQ (population-level), environment still matters.
optWhy.B: 0.70 is population-level concordance, not 70% of an individual's IQ.
optWhy.C: Shared rearing environment still matters.
optWhy.D: MZ twins are genetically near-identical (essentially clones).

stem: A study reports heritability of depression = 0.40 in a high-stress environment but 0.10 in a low-stress environment. This shows that:

options.text: Heritability is environment-dependent (GxE); genetic influence on depression is larger under high stress
Depression is 40% genetic in all environments

why: Different heritability across environments (0.40 high-stress vs 0.10 low-stress) demonstrates gene-environment interaction: genetic influence on depression is larger under high stress. Heritability is not 40% in all environments, depression is not entirely environmental, and genes do influence depression.

optWhy.A: Correct. Heritability is environment-dependent (GxE); genetic influence larger under high stress.
optWhy.B: Heritability is 0.40 only in high-stress, not all environments.
optWhy.C: Depression is not entirely environmental (heritability > 0).
optWhy.D: Genes do influence depression (heritability > 0).

stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Gene-environment correlation means people's genotypes correlate with the environments they experience.
reason: People actively select, evoke, or create environments that correlate with their genotype (passive, evocative, active rGE).

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false
Assertion is false but Reason is true

why: Both are true and the Reason explains the Assertion: gene-environment correlation (rGE) means genotypes correlate with experienced environments because people select/evoke/create environments matched to their genotype (passive, evocative, active).

optWhy.A: Correct. Both true; rGE mechanisms (passive, evocative, active) explain genotype-environment correlation.
optWhy.B: The Reason is the correct explanation.
optWhy.C: The Reason is true.
optWhy.D: The Assertion is true.

stem: Gene-environment interaction means that:

options.text: Different genotypes respond differently to the same environment
Genes determine behavior independently of environment
Environment determines behavior independently of genes

why: Gene-environment interaction (GxE) means different genotypes respond differently to the same environment (e.g., some people are more sensitive to stress). Genes do not determine behavior independently of environment; environment does not determine behavior independently of genes; genes and environment do interact.

optWhy.A: Correct. GxE = different genotypes respond differently to the same environment.
optWhy.B: Genes do not determine behavior independently of environment.
optWhy.C: Environment does not determine behavior independently of genes.
optWhy.D: Genes and environment do interact (that is GxE).

stem: The diathesis-stress model proposes that a disorder develops when:

options.text: A genetic vulnerability (diathesis) combines with environmental stress
A genetic vulnerability alone is sufficient

why: The diathesis-stress model: a disorder develops when a predisposing vulnerability (diathesis, often genetic) combines with environmental stress. Neither alone is necessarily sufficient; neither genes nor environment is irrelevant.

optWhy.A: Correct. Diathesis (vulnerability) + stress (environment) -> disorder.
optWhy.B: Genetic vulnerability alone is not sufficient; stress is needed.
optWhy.C: Environmental stress alone is not sufficient; vulnerability is needed.
optWhy.D: Both genes and environment matter.

stem: Match the term (List-I) to its definition (List-II).
listII: 2. Proportion of population variation due to genes
3. Different genotypes respond differently to same environment
why: Heritability = proportion of population variation due to genes (2); genotype = genetic makeup/alleles (4); phenotype = observable characteristic (1); gene-environment interaction = different genotypes respond differently to same environment (3).

optWhy.A: Correct. A-2 (heritability), B-4 (genotype), C-1 (phenotype), D-3 (GxE).
optWhy.B: Genotype is genetic makeup (4), not heritability (2).
optWhy.C: Genotype is genetic makeup (4), not observable characteristic (1).
optWhy.D: Heritability is proportion of variation (2), not GxE (3).

stem: Which statements are correct?
statements: 1. Monozygotic twins share nearly 100% of their genes; dizygotic twins share about 50%.
2. Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked cause of intellectual disability.
3. Higher MZ than DZ concordance proves a trait is entirely genetic.
4. Gene-environment correlation means people select environments matched to their genotype.
why: Statement 1 is correct (MZ ~100%, DZ ~50% shared genes). Statement 2 is correct (Fragile X = X-linked intellectual disability). Statement 3 is incorrect: higher MZ concordance does not prove entirely genetic (MZ concordance rarely 100%). Statement 4 is correct (rGE = people select environments matched to genotype).

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 2 and 4.
optWhy.C: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 1 and 4.
optWhy.D: Statement 3 is false; higher MZ concordance does not prove entirely genetic.

stem: Match the chromosomal anomaly (List-I) to its typical feature (List-II).
why: Down syndrome = trisomy 21 (1); Turner = 45,X females (short stature, webbed neck) (2); Klinefelter = 47,XXY males (tall, reduced fertility) (3); XYY = 47,XYY males, not a criminal syndrome (4).

optWhy.A: Correct. A-1 (Down), B-2 (Turner), C-3 (Klinefelter), D-4 (XYY).
optWhy.B: Down is trisomy 21 (1), not 45,X (2).
optWhy.C: Turner is 45,X (2), not 47,XXY (3); Klinefelter is 47,XXY (3), not 45,X (2).
optWhy.D: XYY is 47,XYY males not a criminal syndrome (4), not Down (1); Down is trisomy 21 (1), not XYY.

stem: Which statements are correct?
statements: 1. Heritability is environment-dependent (changes if environmental variation changes).
2. A trait can have high heritability yet still be modifiable by environment.
3. High heritability means a trait cannot be changed by intervention.
4. Adoption and twin studies are the classic methods to estimate heritability.
why: Statement 1 is correct (heritability is environment-dependent). Statement 2 is correct (high heritability does not preclude environmental modification). Statement 3 is incorrect: high heritability does NOT mean a trait cannot be changed by intervention. Statement 4 is correct (adoption/twin studies estimate heritability).

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 2 and 4.
optWhy.C: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 1 and 4.
optWhy.D: Statement 3 is false; high heritability does not mean unchangeable by intervention.

stem: Which statements are correct?
statements: 1. Molecular genetics can identify specific genes associated with behavior, but effects are typically small.
2. Most behavioral traits are polygenic (many genes, small effects).
3. A 'gene for' a complex behavior usually exists with large effect.
4. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) typically find many small-effect variants.
5. The nature-nurture debate is resolved in favor of genes.
why: Statement 1 is correct (molecular genetics finds small-effect genes). Statement 2 is correct (most behavioral traits are polygenic). Statement 3 is incorrect: there is generally no single 'gene for' a complex behavior with large effect. Statement 4 is correct (GWAS finds many small-effect variants). Statement 5 is incorrect: nature-nurture is not resolved in favor of genes; it is interaction.

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct; statements 3 and 5 are false.
optWhy.B: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 1 and 4.
optWhy.C: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 1 and 4.
optWhy.D: Statements 3 and 5 are false.

stem: A patient with Parkinson's disease (substantia nigra dopamine loss) shows rigidity and bradykinesia. The best neurochemical explanation is:

options.text: Dopamine loss in the nigrostriatal pathway impairs movement initiation
Acetylcholine excess at the neuromuscular junction
Serotonin excess in the raphe nuclei

why: Parkinson's disease results from dopaminergic neuron loss in the substantia nigra pars compacta, reducing dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway to the striatum, impairing movement initiation (rigidity, tremor, bradykinesia). It is not due to acetylcholine excess at the NMJ, serotonin excess, or GABA deficiency in the cerebellum.

optWhy.A: Correct. Dopamine loss in the nigrostriatal pathway impairs movement initiation.
optWhy.B: Acetylcholine excess at the NMJ is not the mechanism of Parkinson's.
optWhy.C: Serotonin excess in the raphe nuclei is not the mechanism.
optWhy.D: GABA deficiency in the cerebellum is not the mechanism of Parkinson's.

stem: A researcher wants to map task-related brain activity with millisecond precision. The best choice is:

options.text: fMRI (good spatial resolution but slow hemodynamic response)

why: EEG has millisecond temporal resolution, ideal for tracking rapid neural dynamics. fMRI has good spatial resolution but a slow hemodynamic (BOLD) response (seconds), so it cannot resolve millisecond events. CT and structural MRI are anatomical, not functional/timing tools.

optWhy.A: Correct. EEG = millisecond temporal resolution.
optWhy.B: fMRI BOLD is too slow (seconds) for millisecond changes.
optWhy.C: CT is structural/anatomical.
optWhy.D: Structural MRI is anatomical.

stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Higher monozygotic (MZ) than dizygotic (DZ) twin concordance suggests a genetic contribution to a trait.
reason: MZ twins share nearly 100% of their genes, whereas DZ twins share about 50%, so greater MZ concordance indicates genetic influence.

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false
Assertion is false but Reason is true

why: Both are true and the Reason explains the Assertion: MZ twins share ~100% of genes; DZ twins share ~50%. Greater MZ than DZ concordance indicates that genetic similarity tracks trait similarity, supporting a genetic contribution.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both true; MZ/DZ genetic similarity difference explains higher MZ concordance.
optWhy.B: The Reason is the correct explanation.
optWhy.C: The Reason is true.
optWhy.D: The Assertion is true.

stem: Match the neurotransmitter (List-I) to its associated disorder (List-II).
why: Dopamine nigrostriatal loss = Parkinson's (1); serotonin raphe nuclei = depression/anxiety (2); acetylcholine basal forebrain loss = Alzheimer's (3); GABA reduced inhibition = epilepsy (4).

optWhy.A: Correct. A-1 (dopamine Parkinson's), B-2 (serotonin depression/anxiety), C-3 (acetylcholine Alzheimer's), D-4 (GABA epilepsy).
optWhy.B: Dopamine is Parkinson's (1), not depression/anxiety (2).
optWhy.C: Serotonin is depression/anxiety (2), not Alzheimer's (3); acetylcholine is Alzheimer's (3), not depression/anxiety (2).
optWhy.D: GABA is epilepsy (4), not dopamine (4); dopamine is Parkinson's (1), not GABA.

stem: Which statements are correct?
statements: 1. Heritability is a population statistic, not an individual-level value.
2. Heritability of 0.60 means 60% of an individual's IQ is genetic.
3. Adoption and twin studies are used to estimate heritability.
4. Heritability is environment-dependent.
why: Statement 1 is correct (heritability is a population statistic). Statement 2 is incorrect: heritability of 0.60 means 60% of the VARIANCE in a population is genetic, not 60% of an individual's IQ. Statement 3 is correct (adoption/twin studies estimate heritability). Statement 4 is correct (heritability changes with environment).

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct; statement 2 is false.
optWhy.B: Statement 3 is false; omits statements 3 and 4.
optWhy.C: Statement 2 is false; omits statements 1 and 4.
optWhy.D: Statement 2 is false; heritability is not an individual-level value.

stem: An EEG shows low-amplitude mixed-frequency waves with sawtooth waves and muscle atonia. This is:
why: REM sleep is characterized by low-amplitude mixed-frequency EEG, sawtooth waves, rapid eye movements, and muscle atonia. N3 has high-amplitude delta waves; N2 has sleep spindles/K-complexes; wakefulness has alpha/beta.

optWhy.A: Correct. Low-amplitude mixed-frequency + sawtooth waves + muscle atonia = REM sleep.
optWhy.B: N3 = high-amplitude delta waves.
optWhy.C: N2 = sleep spindles and K-complexes.
optWhy.D: Wakefulness = alpha/beta, not sawtooth waves and atonia.

stem: A drug that blocks GABA_A receptors would most likely:
why: GABA_A receptors mediate inhibitory Cl- influx. Blocking them reduces inhibition, leading to increased neuronal excitability (and potentially seizures). It does not increase GABA release, decrease excitability, or block acetylcholine release.

optWhy.A: Correct. Blocking GABA_A reduces inhibition, increasing excitability.
optWhy.B: GABA_A blockade does not increase GABA release.
optWhy.C: Blocking inhibition increases, not decreases, excitability.
optWhy.D: GABA_A blockade does not block acetylcholine release.

stem: Neuroplasticity differs from neurogenesis in that:

options.text: Neuroplasticity is broader (includes reorganization), whereas neurogenesis is specifically new neuron formation
Neuroplasticity occurs only in development, neurogenesis only in adulthood

why: Neuroplasticity is the broad capacity of the nervous system to reorganize structure and function (including synaptic changes, cortical remapping). Neurogenesis is specifically the formation of new neurons (a subset of plasticity, mainly in the dentate gyrus and olfactory bulb in adults). They are not synonyms, and neither is restricted to only development or only adulthood.

optWhy.A: Correct. Neuroplasticity is broader; neurogenesis is specifically new neuron formation.
optWhy.B: Neuroplasticity is not only developmental; neurogenesis is not only adult.
optWhy.C: Neuroplasticity is broader than neurogenesis, not vice versa.
optWhy.D: They are distinct concepts, not synonyms.

stem: Chronic stress (high cortisol) can suppress the reproductive axis because:

options.text: Cortisol has no effect on reproduction
Cortisol only affects the HPA axis

why: Chronic stress activates the HPA axis (cortisol), which suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis, reducing GnRH, LH/FSH, and sex-hormone output (and thus reproductive behavior). Cortisol does not stimulate the HPG axis, has clear effects, and affects more than the HPA axis.

optWhy.A: Correct. Cortisol inhibits the HPG axis (GnRH/LH/testosterone).
optWhy.B: Cortisol inhibits, not stimulates, the HPG axis.
optWhy.C: Chronic cortisol clearly affects reproduction.
optWhy.D: Cortisol affects the HPG axis too, not only the HPA axis.

stem: Which statements are correct?
statements: 1. The amygdala is central to fear conditioning.
2. The hippocampus provides context for emotional memories.
3. The hypothalamus mediates autonomic/endocrine expression of emotion.
4. The thalamus is the primary site of emotional experience.
why: Statement 1 is correct (amygdala central to fear conditioning). Statement 2 is correct (hippocampus provides emotional context/declarative memory). Statement 3 is correct (hypothalamus mediates autonomic/endocrine expression). Statement 4 is incorrect: the thalamus is a sensory relay, not the primary site of emotional experience.

optWhy.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct; statement 4 is false.
optWhy.B: Statement 4 is false; omits statements 2 and 3.
optWhy.C: Statement 1 is correct; statement 4 is false.
optWhy.D: Statement 4 is false; thalamus is a relay, not the primary site of emotional experience.

stem: A patient with bilateral hippocampal damage shows:

options.text: Impaired formation of new declarative memories (anterograde amnesia), with preserved old memories

why: Bilateral hippocampal damage (e.g., patient H.M.) causes anterograde amnesia (inability to form new declarative memories) while sparing old consolidated memories and non-declarative learning. It does not cause loss of all memory, inability to feel emotion, or loss of motor control.

optWhy.A: Correct. Bilateral hippocampal damage → anterograde amnesia, old memories spared.
optWhy.B: Not all memory is lost (old memories and non-declarative learning spared).
optWhy.C: Emotion is not abolished (amygdala intact).
optWhy.D: Motor control is not impaired.

stem: Twin studies show high IQ heritability, while lesion studies show specific brain areas affect cognition. Together these indicate:

options.text: Both genes and specific brain systems contribute to cognition
Brain lesions have no effect on IQ

why: Twin studies indicate genetic influence on IQ; lesion studies show specific brain areas are necessary for cognition. Together, both genes and brain systems contribute to cognition. IQ is neither entirely genetic nor entirely environmental, and lesions do affect cognition.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both genes and specific brain systems contribute to cognition.
optWhy.B: IQ is not entirely genetic; environment matters.
optWhy.C: IQ is not entirely environmental; genes matter.
optWhy.D: Brain lesions do affect cognition.

key: Genes and brain systems contribute to cognition

stem: A heritability estimate of 0.50 for a trait means:

options.text: Half of the variation in that trait in the population is attributable to genetic variation
Half of an individual's trait is genetic
The trait is 50% determined by genes in every environment
The trait cannot be changed by environment

why: Heritability of 0.50 means 50% of the VARIATION in that trait in the population is attributable to genetic variation. It is not 50% of an individual's trait, not 50% in every environment, and does not mean the trait cannot be changed by environment.

optWhy.A: Correct. Heritability = proportion of population variation due to genetic variation.
optWhy.B: Heritability is not the proportion of an individual's trait that is genetic.
optWhy.C: Heritability is environment-dependent, not fixed at 50% in every environment.
optWhy.D: Heritable traits can still be modified by environment.

stem: Match the brain structure (List-I) to its primary function (List-II).
why: Hippocampus = declarative memory formation (1); amygdala = fear processing (2); hypothalamus = homeostasis/autonomic-endocrine control (3); basal ganglia = movement initiation/inhibition (4).

optWhy.A: Correct. A-1 (hippocampus memory), B-2 (amygdala fear), C-3 (hypothalamus homeostasis), D-4 (basal ganglia movement).
optWhy.B: Hippocampus is memory (1), not fear (2).
optWhy.C: Hypothalamus is homeostasis (3), not fear (2); amygdala is fear (2), not homeostasis (3).
optWhy.D: Basal ganglia is movement (4), not hippocampus (4); hippocampus is memory (1), not basal ganglia.

stem: A study finds that people who drink more coffee have lower depression rates and concludes coffee prevents depression. The main methodological flaw is:

options.text: Correlation does not imply causation (confounds, reverse causality)

why: An observational association (coffee drinking <-> lower depression) does not establish causation; there may be confounds (e.g., socioeconomic status) or reverse causality (less depression -> more coffee). It does not prove coffee prevents depression, the sample size being large is not a flaw, and depression causing coffee drinking is only one possible reverse-causal explanation, not the main flaw.

optWhy.A: Correct. Correlation does not imply causation; confounds/reverse causality possible.
optWhy.B: An association does not prove coffee prevents depression.
optWhy.C: A large sample is not a methodological flaw.
optWhy.D: Reverse causality is one possibility, but the main flaw is that correlation does not imply causation.

stem: After a stroke damaging the left motor cortex, a patient regains some right-hand movement. The best explanation is:

options.text: Cortical reorganization/neuroplasticity (adjacent areas take over function)
The right motor cortex took over left-hand function
No recovery is possible after stroke

why: Stroke recovery is explained by cortical reorganization/neuroplasticity (adjacent cortical areas take over some function, synaptic changes). CNS neurons do not regenerate completely; the right motor cortex controls the left hand, not right-hand function; recovery after stroke is possible.

optWhy.A: Correct. Cortical reorganization/neuroplasticity explains stroke recovery.
optWhy.B: CNS neurons do not regenerate completely.
optWhy.C: The right motor cortex controls the left hand, not the right hand.
optWhy.D: Recovery after stroke is possible via neuroplasticity.

stem: Sensation differs from perception in that:

options.text: Sensation is the detection of stimuli by receptors; perception is the interpretation/organization of those sensations
Sensation is interpretation; perception is detection
Sensation occurs only in the cortex

why: Sensation is the detection of stimuli by sensory receptors (transduction); perception is the interpretation/organization of those sensations into meaningful experience. They are not synonyms, and sensation begins at receptors (not only in the cortex).

optWhy.A: Correct. Sensation = detection by receptors; perception = interpretation/organization.
optWhy.B: This reverses sensation and perception.
optWhy.C: They are distinct processes, not synonyms.
optWhy.D: Sensation begins at peripheral receptors, not only in the cortex.

stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Gene-environment interaction means different genotypes respond differently to the same environment.
reason: Genotypes vary in their sensitivity to environmental influences (differential susceptibility).

options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false
Assertion is false but Reason is true

why: Both are true and the Reason explains the Assertion: gene-environment interaction means that different genotypes respond differently to the same environment because genotypes vary in their sensitivity/differential susceptibility to environmental influences.

optWhy.A: Correct. Both true; differential sensitivity explains why genotypes respond differently.
optWhy.B: The Reason is the correct explanation.
optWhy.C: The Reason is true.
optWhy.D: The Assertion is true.

stem: To test whether the hippocampus is necessary for spatial memory, the best approach is:

options.text: Hippocampal lesion (or reversible inactivation) then test spatial memory
Measure heart rate during spatial memory

why: Necessity is established by removing/inactivating the hippocampus and testing whether spatial memory is impaired (lesion/inactivation = causal test). fMRI shows correlation, not necessity; heart rate is unrelated; systemic drug administration is not hippocampus-specific.

optWhy.A: Correct. Hippocampal lesion/inactivation tests necessity causally.
optWhy.B: fMRI shows correlation, not causal necessity.
optWhy.C: Heart rate is unrelated to hippocampal necessity.
optWhy.D: Systemic drug administration is not hippocampus-specific.

stem: In a split-brain patient (corpus callosum severed), an object is shown in the LEFT visual field. The patient:

options.text: Cannot name it verbally but can point to it with the left hand
Can name it but not point to it
Can both name and point to it normally

why: The left visual field projects to the right hemisphere. With the corpus callosum severed, the right hemisphere (which perceives the object) cannot communicate with the left-hemisphere language centers, so the patient cannot name it. The left hand is controlled by the right hemisphere, so the patient can point to the object with the left hand. Perception is intact; naming and pointing are dissociated.

optWhy.A: Correct. Right hemisphere perceives (left visual field) but cannot name (language in left, disconnected); left hand (right hemisphere) can point.
optWhy.B: Cannot name, so naming is impaired.
optWhy.C: The disconnection prevents normal naming.
optWhy.D: The right hemisphere perceives the object, so perception is intact.
